challenges.name: http-caching-quiz
challenges.title: Read the cache headers
challenges.description: Three statements about Rice Rocket's CDN and browser caching after a week of production traffic. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: Work out the response's age at the CDN, then compare it with the freshness lifetime (s-maxage) and with lifetime + stale-while-revalidate.
Read RFC 9111's definitions of `no-cache` and `no-store`: which one forbids storing, and which one forbids using a stored copy without checking first?
A shared cache keys responses by URL (plus Vary). What does a cached `/api/cart` response contain, and who asks for that URL next?

questions.question:
The menu API answers through the CDN with:

```text
Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300
```

The CDN stored the menu 90 seconds ago. A customer opens the restaurant.

Statement: "The CDN answers at once with the stored menu and fetches a fresh copy from the origin in the background, because 90 s is past the 60 s lifetime but inside the 300 s stale-while-revalidate window."
questions.explanation: True. At 90 s the response is stale (age > s-maxage 60) but within lifetime + stale-while-revalidate (60 + 300 s), so RFC 5861 lets the cache serve the stored copy immediately and revalidate asynchronously. The next customer gets the refreshed menu. Past 360 s the CDN must wait for the origin. The misconception is that a stale response always costs the user a round trip to the origin.

questions.question:
The HTML of the restaurant pages is sent with:

```text
Cache-Control: no-cache
ETag: "r42-5f1c"
```

Statement: "`no-cache` means neither the browser nor the CDN stores the page, so every visit downloads the full HTML again."
questions.explanation: False. `no-cache` allows storing but requires validation before every reuse: the cache sends `If-None-Match: "r42-5f1c"` and gets a small `304 Not Modified` while the page is unchanged, or the new page right after a deploy. The directive that forbids storing is `no-store`. The misconception comes from the name; `no-cache` is cheap revalidation, not no caching.

questions.question:
Support received screenshots of a customer seeing someone else's cart. The cart API was answering with:

```text
GET /api/cart   (cookie: session=...)
Cache-Control: public, max-age=30
```

```text
CDN log
12:01:03  /api/cart  MISS  -> origin (session of An)
12:01:11  /api/cart  HIT   age=8   (session of Binh)
```

Statement: "`private` (or `no-store`) keeps the CDN from storing the cart; the browser may still keep a `private` response for its own user."
questions.explanation: True. The CDN keys the entry by URL, so Binh received An's cart from the shared cache. `private` tells shared caches not to store the response while the user's own browser still may; `no-store` forbids storing anywhere. Personalized responses (carts, profiles, anything decided by a cookie or token) must never be `public`. The misconception is that a session cookie on the request makes the CDN bypass its cache.

challenges.name: caching-headers
challenges.title: Set the caching headers for each route
challenges.description: Rice Rocket's Next.js app answered everything with the framework defaults: the hashed bundles were revalidated on every visit, menu edits took minutes to appear, and once a misconfigured rule let the CDN serve one customer's cart to another. The editor holds `middleware.js` with the header rules missing, each marked by a `// [ ]` line; some pieces are wrong on purpose. Fill every line so that: hashed files under `/_next/static/` are cached for a year and never revalidated; a restaurant's menu (`/api/restaurants/<id>/menu`) is shared by the CDN, at most 60 s old when served fresh, and refreshed in the background for up to 300 s after that, while browsers always check with the CDN; the cart (`/api/cart`) is never stored anywhere; restaurant pages (`/restaurants/...`) are stored but checked on every visit; anything else is not stored. The browser reads `Cache-Control`; the CDN reads `CDN-Cache-Control` when present. Run plays timelines of requests from several customers through their browsers, the CDN and the origin.
hints: For each route ask three questions: may a shared cache store it, how long is it fresh, and what may happen once it is stale?

Look at `immutable`, `max-age`, `no-cache`, `no-store`, `private` and `stale-while-revalidate`, and at how `CDN-Cache-Control` lets the CDN and the browser follow different rules for the same response.

A product API on another site: `if (path.startsWith("/api/products/")) return { "Cache-Control": "no-cache", "CDN-Cache-Control": "max-age=120, stale-while-revalidate=600" };` and an account endpoint: `if (path === "/api/me") return { "Cache-Control": "private, no-store" };`

tests.name: A hashed bundle is downloaded once and then served from the browser
A menu edit reaches customers about a minute later; the CDN refreshes in the background
Each customer only ever sees their own cart
Pages are checked on every visit: 304 while unchanged, the new deploy at once
Lunch rush: 4 customers in 50 s cost the origin one menu request
